entries.modern_form: Mann's *dhus- (1) 'whirr, buzz; whirring object, spindle' (IEC 224); no such root in Pokorny, Walde-Pokorny or Watkins/AHD
entries.note: Nourai copies Mann faithfully: An Indo-European Comparative Dictionary p. 224 heads exactly 'dhus- (1) “whirr, buzz; whirring object, spindle”. Cf. WP I, 564 & 844' and lists under it 'Per. dük (“spindle”. For -k cf. Per. xūk “pig”, fr. *sūs); Gk. cf. thus-thia “Bacchanalian rods”; Lat. fūsus “spindle”; MHG cf. tūsen “rush, roar, ring”; Sw. düs “carousal”'. So the root box, its language label and its gloss reproduce a real (if idiosyncratic) reference. The reservation is that this root is Mann's alone. Walde-Pokorny I 843-846 does have a root 'dheues-, dhues-, dheus-, dhus- „stieben, stäuben, wirbeln“' (= Pokorny 268-271), but neither WP nor Pokorny nor Watkins lists any spindle word under it, and the two words Nourai hangs on it are exactly the two whose etymology the standard handbooks call unknown (Latin fūsus) or unstated (Persian dūk). Mann habitually creates such semantically narrow roots by abstracting from two or three isolated words; treat the box as a hypothesis, not an established PIE root.

nodes.derivation: New Persian دوک dūk 'spindle' is the regular continuation of Middle Persian dōk, written dwk' in Book Pahlavi and glossed 'spindle' by MacKenzie (Concise Pahlavi Dictionary p. 27: 'dōk [dwk' | N ~] spindle'); Wiktionary derives the Persian word from exactly that Middle Persian form. Middle Persian ō regularly gives New Persian ū (majhūl wāw > maʿrūf in classical NP, cf. MP rōz > NP rūz), so dōk > dūk is unproblematic. What is not established is the step drawn in the chart, root → Persian: no Old or Middle Iranian ancestor beyond MP dōk is attested, and neither Horn nor Hübschmann nor Aryanpur has an entry for the word. Mann's phonetic argument for the -k ('for -k cf. Per. xūk “pig”, fr. *sūs') is weak: xūk goes back to Old Iranian *hū-ka- with the productive suffix *-ka-, so the -k is a suffix, not a reflex of the root-final consonant — which means dūk would have to be *dū-ka-, an unattested stem. Verdict: the Persian word and its Middle Persian ancestor are real and correctly glossed; only the PIE affiliation is Mann's conjecture.
nodes.derivation_fa: «دوک» فارسی نو دنبالهٔ منظمِ فارسی میانهٔ dōk (نوشتهٔ پهلوی dwk′) است که مکنزی در «فرهنگ کوچک پهلوی» ص ۲۷ آن را «spindle/دوک» معنی کرده؛ ویکی‌واژه نیز فارسی «دوک» را از همین صورتِ پهلوی می‌گیرد. اوی مجهولِ فارسی میانه در فارسی دری به اوی معروف بدل شده (مانند rōz > rūz)، پس dōk > dūk دگرگونیِ آواییِ عادی است. آنچه اثبات‌نشده مانده پیوند این واژه با ریشهٔ هندواروپاییِ *dʰus- است: نه صورتی ایرانی باستان از آن به‌جا مانده و نه هرن و هوبشمان و آریان‌پور مدخلی برایش دارند. استدلالِ مان دربارهٔ ـک پایانی (قیاس با «خوک» از *sūs) هم سست است، زیرا کافِ «خوک» پسوندِ *-ka- ایرانی باستان است نه بازماندهٔ صامتِ ریشه. پس: خودِ واژه و صورتِ پهلویِ آن درست است، ولی ریشه‌شناسیِ هندواروپاییِ نورایی (به نقل از مان) تنها یک حدس است.

nodes.derivation: Latin fūsus, -ī m. 'spindle' (whence It. fuso, Sp. huso, Fr. fuseau) is real and correctly glossed, but no modern authority derives it from anything. Ernout-Meillet, Dictionnaire étymologique de la langue latine p. 470, s.v. fūsus: 'fuseau; employé surtout au pl. Attesté depuis Catulle, mais sans doute ancien. – Panroman … Étymologie inconnue.' Buck §6.32 says the same and adds that the obvious link with fundere is unusable: 'Lat. fūsus (> Romance words), etym. dub. Connection with fundere “pour” difficult semantically'; Wiktionary calls the origin 'unclear, possibly from a non-Indo-European substrate'. Mann's assignment to *dhus- founders on Latin phonology as well: PIE *dh- gives Latin f- only word-initially before a vowel, which is fine, but there is no trace of the *-s- of the root in a form whose -s- is intervocalic (*dhus-o- should give **fūror-/**fūr-, by rhotacism, not fūsus). The chart's own NOTE is also inaccurate: Pokorny p.448 does not derive the spindle from ǵheu- 'to pour'. Under the extension gheud- he writes 'lat. fundō, -ere, fūdī, fūsum „gieße …“ (über fūsus „Spindel“ s. WH. I 474)' — the fūsum on that page is the perfect participle of fundō, and Pokorny expressly refers the homophonous noun fūsus 'spindle' away to Walde-Hofmann; Walde-Pokorny I (s.v. gheud-) is even blunter: 'kaum fusus „Spindel“?'. So modern scholarship rejects both Nourai's derivation and the alternative he reports.
nodes.derivation_fa: لاتینِ fūsus «دوک» واژه‌ای واقعی است، اما ریشه‌شناسیِ پذیرفته‌ای ندارد: ارنو و مِیه در «فرهنگ ریشه‌شناختی زبان لاتین» ص ۴۷۰ صریحاً می‌نویسند «Étymologie inconnue» (ریشه ناشناخته)، باک در بخش ۶٫۳۲ آن را «مشکوک» می‌خواند و می‌افزاید پیوندش با fundere «ریختن» از نظر معنایی دشوار است، و ویکی‌واژه احتمال وام از زیرلایه‌ای غیرهندواروپایی را مطرح می‌کند. فرضِ مان (و به تبع او نورایی) از نظر آواییِ لاتین هم لنگ می‌زند، چون سینِ میان‌واکه‌ایِ *dhus-o- در لاتین باید به ر بدل می‌شد (قانون rhotacism) و **furus می‌داد نه fūsus. یادداشتِ خودِ نمودار هم نادرست است: پوکورنی در ص ۴۴۸ نه fūsus «دوک» بلکه fūsum (اسم مفعولِ fundō) را از ریشهٔ *ǵheu- «ریختن» می‌گیرد و دربارهٔ «دوک» می‌نویسد «برای fūsus به معنی Spindel نگاه کنید به Walde‑Hofmann ج۱ ص۴۷۴»؛ والده‑پوکورنی نیز می‌نویسد «به‌سختی fusus „Spindel“». پس پژوهش امروزی هر دو ریشه‌شناسی را رد می‌کند.

entries.note: The root itself, its language label and its gloss are exactly right. Pokorny IEW 278 (the very page Nourai cites; POK_01.txt line 3993, immediately after the page marker '278') heads 'dhu̯ē̆r-, dhu̯ō̆r-, dhur-, dhur̥- „Tür“', and Watkins/AHD has 'dhwer-. Door, doorway (usually in plural). Originally an apophonic noun *dhwor-, *dhur- … [Pok. dhu̯ér- 278.]'; Wiktionary's *dʰwer- page cites Pokorny 278-279, Mallory-Adams (EIEC 168 f. *dhu̯ṓr), NIL 130-135, Kroonen, de Vaan and Beekes for the same reconstruction. The defect is the middle name of the box: 'Dhrugh' does not belong to the door root. *dhrugh- is the zero grade of *dhreugh- 'to deceive' (Pokorny 276; POK_01 line 4011 sets out the series dhuer-gh- : dhurgh- : dhrugh- : dhreugh- under the homonymous root dhu̯er- 'durch Täuschung zu Fall bringen', IEW 277) — which Nourai himself heads as a SEPARATE root on the preceding page (pdf 135, 'Dhreugh : to deceive', refs POK:276) with Av. draoga-, OP duruj- and NP دروغ under it. So the same author files *dhrugh- twice, once correctly and once here. The slip is his own and deliberate enough to have generated the index redirect 'Dhrugh → Dhwer' on p. 105 of the book; its likely origin is Kent's lexicon, where duruj- 'lie, deceive' with 'pIE *dhrugh-' stands on the same opening (pp. 191-192) as duvara- 'door'. I rendered the printed page (pdf 136, saved as data/verification/sources/refs/ocr/BOOK/136.png) and the book does print 'Dhwer, Dhrugh, Dhwor : door' — the extraction is faithful; the error is the book's. No node on the page actually descends from *dhrugh-, so nothing else in the chart is affected.
entries.note_fa: خودِ ریشه و برچسبِ زبان و معنای آن درست است: پوکورنی در همان صفحه‌ای که نورایی ارجاع می‌دهد (ص ۲۷۸) سرواژهٔ «dhu̯ē̆r-, dhu̯ō̆r-, dhur-, dhur̥- „Tür/در“» را آورده و واتکینز نیز ذیل dhwer- «در، درگاه (بیشتر به صورت جمع)» همین را با ارجاع به پوکورنی ۲۷۸ ثبت کرده است. اشکال در نامِ میانیِ جعبه است: *dhrugh- به این ریشه ربطی ندارد، بلکه صورتِ صفرِ ریشهٔ *dhreugh- «فریفتن» است (پوکورنی ۲۷۶) — همان ریشه‌ای که خودِ نورایی در صفحهٔ پیشین (۱۰۵) جداگانه با نامِ Dhreugh و با واژه‌های اوستاییِ draoga-، پارسی باستانِ duruj و «دروغ» فارسی آورده است. سرچشمهٔ این لغزش احتمالاً فرهنگِ کِنت است که در همان دو صفحهٔ ۱۹۱ـ۱۹۲ هم duruj- «دروغ گفتن» با ریشهٔ *dhrugh- و هم duvara- «در» را آورده. تصویرِ صفحهٔ چاپی را دیدم: کتاب واقعاً «Dhwer, Dhrugh, Dhwor : door» چاپ کرده، پس خطا از خوانشِ اسکن نیست، خطای خودِ کتاب است. چون هیچ گرهی روی این صفحه از *dhrugh- گرفته نشده، بقیهٔ نمودار آسیب نمی‌بیند.

nodes.derivation: Both citation forms are correct. Avestan dvar- (consonant stem, acc. sg. dvarəm, loc. dvarə) means 'gate, court; mountain pass' — Bartholomae, Altiranisches Wörterbuch 766, and the phrase quoted throughout the AIW, 'upa dvarəm xšaθrō.sukəm apanōtəməm', 'at the pass Xšaθrō.suka, the highest-lying one' (Yt. 5.54, BRT.txt lines 3553, 9048, 10770). Old Persian duvara- 'door, gate, court' is attested in the locative-with-postposed-ā duvarayā, e.g. DB 2.75 duvarayā-maiy basta adāriya 'he was held bound at my court/gate' (Kent, Old Persian p. 192 and §191.I); the same stem gives duvarθi- 'portico, colonnade' < *dvara-varθi- by haplology (Kent §129). Phonetically both continue PIE *dʰwer-/*dʰwor-: Old Persian regularly breaks the initial cluster with an anaptyctic u (dv- > duv-, cf. duvitīya- 'second' beside Av. bitya-), while Avestan keeps dv-; Indo-Iranian *dhw- lost its aspiration early in the weak cases (Skt. nom. pl. dvā́raḥ beside acc. pl. duráḥ), which is why Sanskrit shows d- and not dh-.
nodes.derivation_fa: هر دو صورتِ نقل‌شده درست است. در اوستا dvar- (ستاکِ صامتی، رایی dvarəm، دری dvarə) به معنی «در، دروازه، حیاط؛ گذرگاهِ کوهستانی» است — بارتولمه، «فرهنگ ایرانی باستان» ستون ۷۶۶، با شاهدِ مکررِ «upa dvarəm xšaθrō.sukəm» «بر گذرگاهِ خْشَثْروسوکَ» (یشت ۵٫۵۴). در پارسی باستان duvara- «در، بارگاه» در صورتِ دریِ duvarayā آمده، چنان‌که در بیستون ۲٫۷۵ «duvarayā-maiy basta adāriya» «او را بسته بر درگاهِ من نگاه داشتند» (کِنت، ص ۱۹۲). از نظر آوایی هر دو دنبالهٔ *dʰwer-/*dʰwor- هندواروپایی‌اند: در پارسی باستان خوشهٔ آغازینِ dv- با واکهٔ میانجیِ u شکسته شده (duv-، مانند duvitīya-)، حال آنکه اوستایی dv- را نگه داشته است. ادعای نورایی در این گره کاملاً درست است.

nodes.derivation: dar «در» is confirmed: Old Iranian *dwar- > Middle Persian dar (Book Pahlavi ideogram BBA < Aramaic bb', phonetic dl; MacKenzie 1971 p. 25 'dar [BBA; dl | M dr, N =] door; palace; chapter, subject') > NP dar; Horn, Grundriss §545 gives precisely 'der “Tür”; … ap. duvar- “Tür”, duvarayā; aw. dvar-; phlv. dar, dargas; ai. dvār-, durās; arm. durn' and adds the dialect forms (kurd. bar/der, oss. dvar, waχ. bār, šiγn. div/divēr). Wiktionary derives NP در from MP dar citing ESIJa II 500. The two words in the chart's parenthesis belong here too: darvāza «دروازه» 'city gate' (dar + -vāza, Horn §545) and darbān «دربان» 'doorkeeper' (dar + bān 'keeper'; Lokotsch no. 490 'Pers. dārbān “Türhüter” [von pers. dar “Tür” Horn NpEt S. 120, Nr. 545 und -bān]', whence Anglo-Indian durwaun and Rum./Ger. Trabant). darband «دربند» is likewise sound: dar + band 'bar, barrier' (√band, PIE *bhendh-, which is where the chart's ☞Bhendhe points), attested already in Middle Persian — MacKenzie p. 25 'darband [BBA bnd | N ~] gate' — and the name of the Caspian pass-city Darband/Derbent; Addi Shir, al-Alfāẓ al-fārisiyya al-muʿarraba, calls الدربند 'pure Persian … compounded of در i.e. door and بند i.e. bond and barrier'. bandar «بندر» 'seaport' is the weak link: Mo'in gives it no origin tag at all, Dehkhoda offers only a popular gloss ('where they set down goods and gear'), and Wiktionary's Persian entry marks the etymology as missing, noting that an analysis band + dar 'makes phonetic and semantic sense, but is there literature to confirm this?'. The alternative usually met with — band 'dam, dyke, mole' plus a suffix — is equally unproven. Arabic بندر / pl. بنادر (which the chart's parenthesis gives) is certainly borrowed from Persian, so the direction of that arrow is right; only the internal analysis is unsupported. Hence 'plausible' for the node as a whole.

nodes.derivation: Arabic دَرْب darb 'narrow road, mountain pass; gate of a quarter' (pl. durūb) is not from the Arabic root d-r-b 'to train, accustom', and the Arab lexicographers themselves said so: Dehkhoda quotes al-Jawālīqī's al-Muʿarrab to the effect that darb is not originally Arabic and that the Arabs applied it to the narrow passes into Byzantine territory, which served as 'gates'. Nourai's specific source-tradition is Addi Shir, al-Alfāẓ al-fārisiyya al-muʿarraba, who says outright «الدرب تعریب درب(ند) بحذف شطره الأخیر» ('al-darb is the arabicised darband with its last part dropped') and, on the same page, «الدربان … من در ای باب ومن بان ای حافظ» and «الدربند … فارسیٌّ محض … مرکب من در ای باب ومن بند ای رباط وسدّ» — i.e. exactly the Persian → Arabic arrow drawn here. Modern scholarship is divided: Wiktionary derives Arabic دَرْب instead from Ancient Greek Δέρβη, the town in Lycaonia at the Cilician Gates (whence the plural al-durūb for the Taurus passes), with Syriac darbā 'way' and Old Spanish adarve as further offshoots; Lokotsch no. 488 lists 'Ar. darb “Weg, enger Weg”' as the source of Sp./Pg. adarve without assigning it any Persian origin. Since the Persian-origin view is that of the Arabic lexicographers and of the Persianist tradition Nourai follows, while the Greek-toponym view is the one now printed in Wiktionary, the node is best rated plausible rather than confirmed.

nodes.derivation: Persian درب darb 'door, large gate' is indeed the Arabic word taken back into Persian — the round trip the chart draws (Persian dar → Arabic darb → Persian darb). Mo'in's entry, the reference Nourai cites, tags it Arabic and gives the Arabic plural: «(دَ رْ) [ع.] (اِ.) درِ بزرگ، دروازهٔ شهر یا قلعه. ج. دروب.» ('[Arabic] (n.) a large door, the gate of a city or citadel; pl. durūb'). The tell-tale of the round trip is exactly that plural: a native Persian در could not form دروب. In modern usage darb is a formal/administrative synonym of dar (درب ورودی etc.) and is often criticised by Persian purists for that reason. A minority alternative exists: Wiktionary's Persian entry derives درب instead from Middle Persian darbās 'palace' (MacKenzie p. 25 'darbās [dlp's] palace'), citing ESIJa II 502 — that would make the word inherited rather than re-borrowed; but Mo'in, Dehkhoda and the Arabising tradition all treat it as the Arabic form, which is what the chart says.

nodes.derivation: The Sogdian word is δβr, read δβar, 'door, gate' — Gharib's Sogdian Dictionary entry no. 3500, which stands on printed page 138, exactly the page Nourai cites. Gharib gives it in Buddhist, Manichaean and Christian Sogdian with a full case paradigm (nom. -y, acc. -w, abl. -h, loc. -y', pl. -t', obl. pl. -ty) and states its origin as '<Av. duvara', i.e. the same Old Iranian *dwar- that gives Av. dvar- and OP duvara-. Phonetically the node is regular: Old Iranian *dw- becomes Sogdian δβ- (the Manichaean and Christian scripts write db/δβ), and the unstressed final vowel is lost, so *dwara- > δβar. The chart's transliteration 'dbr' is the Sogdian consonantal spelling as Gharib himself prints it in the alternative script column. The only quibble is the arrow's origin: Sogdian δβar continues Proto-Iranian *dwar- directly, not the Avestan/Old Persian form drawn as its parent (the chart hangs it under node #1, which is a convenience of the tree).

nodes.derivation: *durunz is Proto-Germanic, and the form is quoted letter for letter from Nourai's own source: Watkins/AHD s.v. dhwer- has 'Zero-grade form *dhur- in suffixed forms *dhur-n̥s (accusative plural) and *dhur-o- (neuter) respectively in Germanic *durunz and *duram in Old English duru, door (feminine, originally plural), and dor, door (neuter)'. Pokorny 278 says the same in German: 'ags. duru ds. (Akk. Pl. *dhur-n̥s, germ. *durunz, der auch ahd. Dat. Pl. tur-un, -on nach sich zog)'. The derivation is the regular one: PIE zero-grade *dhur- + accusative-plural *-n̥s > Gmc. *-unz (syllabic nasal vocalised to -un-, *s > z by Verner/Germanic voicing), with *dh- > *d- by Grimm's law. The word was a plural in origin — a door was a pair of leaves — which is why Old English duru is a feminine plural in form.

nodes.derivation: The first word is right: Greek θύρα thúrā 'door' is the ā-stem of the zero grade *dhur- (Pokorny 278: 'ā-St. θύρα „Tür“ (hom. meist Pl.)'; Beekes, EDG s.v. θύρα), with the regular Greek development *dh- > th-. The second is not. There is no Greek word thuroidēs behind 'thyroid': the medical term is Modern/Medical Latin thyreoideus, from Greek θυρεοειδής thyreoeidḗs 'shield-shaped', a compound of θυρεός thyreós 'the stone put against a door; (hence) the oblong door-shaped shield' + -οειδής '-shaped' (from εἶδος 'form'). Galen's χόνδρος θυρεοειδής 'shield-shaped cartilage' is the Adam's apple, and the gland was named from the cartilage. Klein spells this out: 'thyroid … lit. “shield-shaped” (anat.) — Medical L. thyreoideus, fr. nodes.derivation: Persian تیروئید tirō'id 'thyroid (gland)' is a 20th-century medical loan from French thyroïde, exactly as drawn. Mo'in — Nourai's reference here — tags it «[فر.]», i.e. borrowed from French, and defines it «غده‌ای است در زیر گلو که ماده‌ای به نام تیروکسین را در خون ترشح می‌کند» ('a gland below the throat which secretes into the blood a substance called thyroxine'). The Persian spelling mirrors the French pronunciation rather than the English: French [tiʁɔid] gives تیروئید with a hamza on the wāw seat to render the -o-ï- hiatus, and the initial تی- reflects French ti-, not English thy- [θaɪ]. The same route gives پاراتیروئید, هیپرتیروئیدی and هیپوتیروئیدی, all of which appear in Mo'in's own text.

nodes.derivation: English thyroid, first attested in the 1690s, is from Modern Latin thyreoides / thyroides, itself the Greek θυρεοειδής 'shield-shaped'; Galen's phrase khondros thyreoeidēs, 'shield-shaped cartilage', named the Adam's apple, and the gland lying against that cartilage took the name in the modern anatomical sense from 1849 (Etymonline). So the English word does come from the Greek node, as the chart draws — via Medical Latin, an intermediate the chart leaves out — and the ultimate root is *dʰur- 'door', through θυρεός 'the stone set against a door; the oblong shield'. Watkins lists THYROID under dhwer-, and Klein under door.

nodes.derivation: Latin has forēs f. pl. 'the (two-leaved) door' — an old consonant stem *dhwor-, remade as an i-stem, the singular foris being secondary — and beside it the two adverbs the chart cites: forās 'out of doors, outwards' (an old accusative plural, *dhwor-n̥s) and forīs 'outside, out of doors' (locative/ablative plural, *dhwor-ois). Pokorny 278: 'lat. Plur. forēs f. „zweiflüglige Tür“ (alter kons. St. *dhuor- zum i-St. umgebildet); der Sg. foris, -is ist sekundär; ō-St. in forās „hinaus“, forīs „draußen, außerhalb“'. Watkins analyses the two adverbs exactly as the chart's parent-child relation needs: '*dhwor-n̥s (accusative plural) in Latin forās … 3. *dhwor-ois (locative plural) in Latin foris'. Ernout-Meillet add the semantic point: the door was the boundary of the household, so 'at the doors' came to mean simply 'outside' — which is why Nourai glosses the node 'outdoors, outside' rather than 'door'. Latin f- from PIE *dh- is the regular word-initial Italic outcome (*dh > *þ > f).

nodes.derivation: foreign is secure: c. 1300 ME forein, from Old French forain 'outside, alien', from Vulgar/Medieval Latin forānus < forāneus 'on the outside', a derivative of Latin forīs 'outside' — Watkins puts FOREIGN under *dhwor-n̥s/forās, Ernout-Meillet list 'forānus (-neus) “étranger”, M.L. 3438-9' among the late derivatives of foris/foras. forest is the standard but not the only account: English forest (late 13th c.) is from Old French forest, from Medieval Latin forestis (silva) 'the outside wood', first in the Capitularies of Charlemagne for the royal woodland outside the enclosed park; Ernout-Meillet cite the same document ('forestis, Diplom. de Childebert … cf. fr. forêt') under foris, and Klein s.v. afforest has 'Late L. forestis (scil. silva), “open woodland”'. But Etymonline records two live competitors: derivation from Latin forum in its legal sense 'court, judgement', i.e. 'land placed under a ban', and influence or origin from a Germanic *forhist / OHG forst 'wooded land'. So one of the two English words hangs on a link that modern scholarship treats as probable rather than settled — hence 'plausible' for the node.
nodes.derivation_fa: «foreign» بی‌اشکال است: از حدودِ ۱۳۰۰ میلادی در انگلیسیِ میانه به صورتِ forein، از فرانسهٔ کهنِ forain «بیرونی، بیگانه»، از لاتینِ مردمی/میانهٔ forāneus «بیرونی»، مشتق از forīs «بیرون»؛ واتکینز نیز FOREIGN را زیر forās می‌آورد. اما «forest» روایتِ رایج دارد نه روایتِ یگانه: از فرانسهٔ کهنِ forest، از لاتینِ میانهٔ forestis (silva) «جنگلِ بیرونی»، نخست در فرمان‌های شارلمانی برای بیشه‌های شاهیِ بیرون از پارکِ محصور — ارنو و مِیه همین سند را ذیلِ foris نقل می‌کنند و کلاین هم می‌نویسد «Late L. forestis (scil. silva) “open woodland”». با این حال اتیمانلاین دو نظرِ رقیب را ثبت کرده است: یکی اشتقاق از forum لاتین به معنای حقوقیِ «دادگاه/حکم» (یعنی «زمینِ زیرِ قُرُق») و دیگری تأثیر یا خاستگاهِ ژرمنیِ *forhist / forst در آلمانیِ کهن. پس یکی از دو واژهٔ این گره به حلقه‌ای بند است که پژوهشِ امروزی آن را «محتمل» می‌داند نه قطعی — و از این‌رو گره «با احتیاط پذیرفتنی» است.
